meta.subject: Information and Communication Technology
meta.chapterTitle: Types and components of computer systems
meta.title: Extended reality: AR and VR

sourceRefs.sections: 1.5.1 (extended reality, augmented reality and virtual reality)

objectives: State what extended reality means and identify AR, VR and MR
Describe how AR combines real surroundings with computer-generated information
Describe how VR uses a headset to create a simulated environment
Give textbook examples of AR and VR in learning, work and everyday life
Compare AR and VR by explaining what the user sees and the equipment used

learn.title: What is extended reality?
learn.body: **Extended reality (XR)** is a name for technologies that change how we experience a real or computer-created environment. The textbook names three forms: **augmented reality (AR)**, **virtual reality (VR)** and **mixed reality (MR)**. This lesson focuses on AR and VR.

learn.alt: Two side-by-side scenes: one shows a person using a handheld screen to see a digital object over a real room; the other shows a person wearing a headset inside a fully imagined underwater world
learn.caption: AR adds digital objects to a real scene; VR surrounds the user with a computer-created scene.
learn.imagePrompt: A clean, child-friendly educational illustration split into two equal scenes with no border or labels. Left: a student holds a plain unbranded tablet and can still see an ordinary classroom behind it; a glowing three-dimensional model of a small bridge appears over the real desk through the tablet display. Right: a student wears a simple plain virtual-reality headset; show a soft cutaway bubble around them containing an immersive underwater world with fish and coral, with the actual room fading outside the bubble. Clear difference between real-world overlay and fully simulated environment. Muted teal and amber palette, no text, no writing, no numbers, no labels, no logos, no brand names.

learn.title: Augmented reality keeps the real world visible
learn.body: **Augmented reality (AR)** adds **digital objects or information** to a view of the **real world**. The extra content might be a picture, moving animation or information on the display. The person can still see what is happening around them and respond to real objects.

learn.title: Key features of AR
items: **Real surroundings remain visible** — the person is not cut off from the physical world
**Digital overlays** — computer-made images, information or animations appear with the real scene
**Viewing devices** — a smartphone, phablet or special goggles can display AR
**Interaction** — the user can continue to move around and deal with real objects

learn.title: AR and VR at a glance

rows.label: What you see
rows.a: Your real surroundings with added digital content
rows.b: A scene made by a computer instead of your real surroundings

rows.label: Feeling of being there
rows.a: You stay aware of the physical world
rows.b: You feel surrounded by the simulated world

rows.label: Example
rows.a: Trying a digital make-up look while seeing your face

rows.label: How you use it
rows.a: Adds details to a place you can still see
rows.b: Lets you look all around a virtual place, often through a 360° view

learn.title: AR for a rescue team
learn.body: A rescue team studies a possible route into a damaged building. An AR view shows a **3D model** of the area. The team can study the layout and practise a rescue plan before entering the real site. This helps the team plan the operation.

learn.title: Uses of augmented reality
items: **Rescue work:** show 3D views of a site to plan and try out procedures
**Shopping:** preview make-up on a face before choosing a product
**Vehicle sales:** explore a digital view of a car interior before buying
**Entertainment:** make digital characters appear in the place around the viewer
**Healthcare:** build 3D views from patient scans to support diagnosis or surgery planning

learn.title: Virtual reality replaces the scene around you
learn.body: **Virtual reality (VR)** puts a person inside a **simulated digital environment**. A **VR headset** or **head-mounted display** shows the virtual world. A **360-degree view** lets the user look in different directions. Unlike AR, the user is visually separated from the normal surroundings.

learn.title: Where virtual reality can be used
items: **Training:** rehearse military tasks or practise a medical operation
**Education and heritage:** explore an old building or historic site without being there
**Healthcare:** use a simulated scene to help with diagnosis or treatment planning
**Business:** practise conversations or workplace situations with role-play
**Engineering:** inspect how a proposed structure may look
**Sport:** practise a movement and receive feedback
**Science:** examine an enlarged digital model of a cell or molecule
**Entertainment and fashion:** experience games or preview a fashion show

learn.title: A VR history trip
learn.body: A class is learning about a building from the past. The students put on VR headsets and move their view around a computer-created version of it. They can explore the inside without travelling to the real building. The surroundings they see are **simulated**, not overlaid on their classroom.

learn.title: To compare, say what happens in both technologies
learn.body: A **compare** answer needs a clear link between AR and VR. Write: "AR adds computer images to the real scene, whereas VR shows a fully digital scene." In **explain** questions, connect the technology to the job: what it shows, then how that helps the named person.

learn.title: Do not swap AR and VR
learn.body: **AR does not usually hide the whole physical world**: it adds digital content to it. **VR does not simply add an object to the room**: it creates the scene the user sees. A VR headset gives an all-around virtual view; a phone or phablet screen can be used to view AR.

check.prompt: Which description best fits augmented reality?
check.hint: Ask whether the person can still observe the physical surroundings while computer-created elements appear in their view.
options: A computer scene completely replaces the surroundings
Digital information is added to a view of a real place
A computer only stores a photograph
A person sees no digital content at all
check.explanation: AR keeps the physical world visible and places computer-created information or objects over it.

check.prompt: Tick (✓) whether each statement describes augmented reality (AR) or virtual reality (VR).
check.hint: For each one, ask: can the user still see the real room, or are they inside a made-up world?

rows.statement: The user sees their room with a digital object added to the view.
rows.explanation: AR adds a virtual layer to the real scene.

rows.statement: A headset shows an all-around simulated world instead of the room.
rows.explanation: VR replaces the surroundings with a digital environment.

rows.statement: A shopper previews a digital make-up look on their face.
rows.explanation: AR can add a digital preview to an image of the real face.

rows.statement: A learner explores a computer-made ancient building as if inside it.
rows.explanation: VR can place the learner within a simulated historic building.

check.explanation: Two correct classifications earn one mark.

check.prompt: Complete each sentence using the most suitable word or phrase. Use each choice only once.
check.hint: Think about how much of the real world the user can still see in AR and in VR.

check.explanation: AR adds to reality, VR replaces the user’s view, and a 360-degree view lets someone look around a virtual environment.

practice.prompt: State the three types of extended reality named in the textbook.

markPoints.point: Augmented reality / AR
Virtual reality / VR
Mixed reality / MR

practice.modelAnswer: Augmented reality is one form of extended reality. Virtual reality is another form. Mixed reality is the third form.
practice.explanation: The textbook lists three XR categories. This unit teaches AR and VR in detail.

practice.prompt: Give two features of augmented reality.

markPoints.point: Adds computer-generated images / data / animation to a real-world view
User can still see / interact with their real surroundings
Can be experienced through goggles / smartphone / phablet screen

practice.modelAnswer: AR puts digital objects over the view of a real place. The user can still see and interact with the physical surroundings.
practice.explanation: Give two different characteristics, not two phrasings of the same overlay feature.

practice.prompt: Describe the equipment and the visual experience used in virtual reality. Give two features and describe what each provides.

markPoints.point: Uses a VR headset / head-mounted display
The headset provides a 360° / all-around view of the computer-generated world
Shows a simulated / computer-created digital environment
The user feels immersed / the real environment is visually replaced
reject: only adds objects to real world

practice.modelAnswer: VR uses a head-mounted headset. It can show the digital scene in every direction. The scene is simulated by a computer. The user feels surrounded by that virtual scene rather than the real room.
practice.explanation: One mark is for each correct feature. A linked description of what it provides earns the second mark.

practice.prompt: A rescue team is planning how to enter a damaged building. Explain how augmented reality could help the team prepare before entering.

markPoints.point: AR can display a 3D image / plan of the area over a real-world view
reject: only a headset showing a fake world

markPoints.point: Rescuers can examine the layout / test rescue steps before entering
Planning in advance helps the team prepare / reduces the risk during the real rescue

practice.modelAnswer: AR can show a 3D view of the damaged building. The rescue team can study the layout and practise the procedure before going inside. This helps them prepare for the real rescue operation.
practice.explanation: Link the digital view to practising procedures and preparing for the actual rescue.

practice.prompt: Students are studying a historic building but cannot visit it. Explain why a virtual reality lesson could help them learn about the building.

markPoints.point: A VR headset displays a simulated / virtual historic building
Students can look around / explore the building as if they were inside it
They can experience it without travelling / being at the real location

practice.modelAnswer: VR can show a computer-created version of the historic building. Students can explore the inside using an all-around view. They can study it without travelling to the real site.
practice.explanation: Explain how VR creates an experience of a building that students cannot visit.

practice.prompt: Compare augmented reality and virtual reality. Your answer must include similarities and differences.

markPoints.point: Both are extended reality / immersive technologies
Both use computer-created / virtual images or environments
AR adds digital objects to the real world whereas VR replaces it with a simulated world
accept: ar shows real world while vr
vr replaces real world while ar
reject: vr only adds to real world
ar shows only a fake world

markPoints.point: AR user can see physical surroundings whereas VR user is separated from them
reject: vr can still see real surroundings

markPoints.point: AR may use a phone / phablet / goggles whereas VR needs a headset
accept: ar can use goggles while vr
phone for ar headset for vr
reject: ar only uses a vr headset

markPoints.point: AR can preview a digital object in a real setting whereas VR can show a complete simulated place

practice.modelAnswer: Both technologies use computer-created information. AR adds virtual objects to a view of the real world, whereas VR shows a complete simulated environment. In AR the user can still see real surroundings, whereas in VR those surroundings are hidden. AR can be viewed on a phone screen, whereas VR uses a headset.
practice.explanation: Each comparison must identify the shared point or state both sides of a difference. The question requires at least one similarity and one difference.

practice.prompt: Give two applications of AR and two applications of VR from the textbook. Label the AR and VR examples.

markPoints.point: AR: trying on / previewing make-up digitally before purchase
AR: 3D images for rescue planning / practising rescue procedures
AR: patient scans into 3D views for diagnosis / surgery
AR: virtual car interior / digital characters added to real situations
VR: training for military / medical operations
VR: explore ancient buildings / heritage places for learning
VR: business role-play / staff training
VR: practise a sport / receive feedback on movement
VR: inspect a digital model of a cell / molecule

practice.modelAnswer: AR can help shoppers preview make-up on their face before buying. AR can also show 3D information for rescue planning. VR can train people to carry out medical procedures. VR can also let students explore an ancient building.
practice.explanation: Give two correct examples for each technology. The examples must be put under the correct AR or VR label.

summary: XR includes augmented reality, virtual reality and mixed reality.
AR adds digital information to the real world, so the user can still see physical surroundings.
AR can support rescue planning, shopping, entertainment and healthcare.
VR uses a headset and a 360-degree view to place the user in a simulated digital environment.
VR can support training, lessons, heritage visits, sport, engineering and scientific models.

flashcards.back: Extended reality, including AR, VR and MR.
Digital information placed over a view of the real world.

flashcards.front: Can an AR user still see the real world?
flashcards.back: Yes. AR adds to the physical surroundings rather than fully replacing them.

flashcards.front: What does a VR headset provide?
flashcards.back: A computer-created environment, often with an all-around 360-degree view.

flashcards.front: Give one AR use from the textbook.
flashcards.back: For example, previewing make-up on a person before buying it.

flashcards.front: Give one VR use from the textbook.
flashcards.back: For example, exploring a simulated ancient building in a history lesson.
